title: Neonatal jaundice
blurb: Spot the babies at risk, choose the right bilirubin test and time frame, care for a baby under phototherapy and act on prolonged jaundice (NICE CG98).
question: On a day 2 home visit, a community midwife notices that Leo, 30 hours old, born at 39 weeks and exclusively breastfed, looks yellow. How quickly should his bilirubin be measured, and with which method?

teach.body: Formally: jaundice is the yellow colouring of the skin and sclerae caused by a raised bilirubin level (hyperbilirubinaemia). In plain English: a newborn breaks down red cells faster than the young liver can clear the pigment, so it builds up in the skin. It is common and usually transient and harmless, and breastfeeding can usually continue (CG98 1.1.1). The midwife's job is to look for it at every opportunity, especially in the first 72 hours, and to know when it is not harmless.

teach.h: Four risk factors for significant jaundice (CG98 1.2.1)
head: Risk factor
What to check
rows: Visible jaundice in the first 24 hours
teach.caption: Babies with any of these need an additional visual inspection by a healthcare professional in the first 48 hours (1.2.9), and breastfeeding mothers need good feeding support (1.2.2).

items: Parents, carers and professionals should all look for jaundice.
Check the naked baby in bright and preferably natural light.
Examine the sclerae and gums, and press lightly to look at blanched skin.
Remember the colour change may be harder to see in darker skin.
Do not rely on visual inspection alone to estimate the level, and do not measure bilirubin routinely in babies who are not visibly jaundiced.

teach.caption: Interpret every result by postnatal age in hours, on the threshold table or graphs (1.2.13). Preterm babies have their own graphs.

teach.h: Caring for a baby under phototherapy (CG98 1.4)
items: Supine, maximum skin exposed, eye protection and routine eye care; thermoneutral environment.
Short breaks of up to 30 minutes for breastfeeding, nappy changes and cuddles (not during intensified phototherapy).
No additional fluids for breastfed babies; mother's expressed milk is the extra feed of choice.
Daily weight and wet nappies to monitor hydration; no white curtains; no sunlight as treatment.
Repeat SBR 4-6 hours after starting, then 6-12 hourly when stable or falling.
Stop when SBR is at least 50 micromol/L below the phototherapy threshold; check for rebound 12-18 hours later.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Leo at home on day 2
teach.body: Leo is 30 hours old, born at 39 weeks, and his mother intends to breastfeed exclusively, so he has a risk factor. He is over 24 hours old, so his bilirubin must be measured within 6 hours. Because he is over 24 hours and over 35 weeks, a transcutaneous bilirubinometer is the right first test. If the TcB reads over 250 micromol/L, the midwife arranges a serum level. She plots the result against his age in hours and supports frequent feeds, waking him if needed (1.3.2).

items.label: Pale chalky stools? Dark urine?
items.sub: measure conjugated bilirubin, FBC, blood group and DAT

teach.caption: Conjugated bilirubin over 25 micromol/L may mean serious liver disease: follow expert advice (1.7.2).

teach.text: Two classic traps. First, a transcutaneous meter is NOT used in the first 24 hours or under 35 weeks: those babies need serum bilirubin. Second, prolonged jaundice is over 14 days for a baby born at 37 weeks or more, but over 21 days for a baby born before 37 weeks. Kernicterus risk rises with SBR over 340 micromol/L (37 weeks+), a rise over 8.5 micromol/L per hour, or signs of encephalopathy (1.5.1).

items: Risk factors: under 38 weeks, sibling had phototherapy, exclusive breastfeeding intended, jaundice in first 24 hours.
Under 24 hours: serum bilirubin within 2 hours, 6-hourly repeats, medical review within 6 hours.
Over 24 hours: measure within 6 hours; TcB if 35 weeks+, serum if TcB over 250.
Phototherapy: supine, eye protection, breaks up to 30 minutes, no extra fluids for breastfed babies.
Prolonged: over 14 days (term) or 21 days (preterm); check stools, urine and conjugated bilirubin.

summary: You can now identify babies at higher risk of significant jaundice, choose serum or transcutaneous measurement and the right time frame, and care safely for a baby under phototherapy. You can also recognise prolonged jaundice and the warning signs of liver disease.

A.q: A midwife is completing the first examination of four babies. Which baby has a NICE CG98 risk factor for significant hyperbilirubinaemia?
options: Born by planned caesarean at 39 weeks
Born at 37+2 weeks gestation
Mother plans mixed formula feeding
Birthweight of 4.2 kg at term
A.why: CG98 1.2.1 lists gestational age under 38 weeks as a risk factor, so a baby born at 37+2 weeks qualifies.

whyNot.0: Caesarean birth is not one of the four CG98 risk factors.
whyNot.2: The listed factor is the mother's intention to breastfeed exclusively, not mixed feeding.
whyNot.3: A large birthweight is not a CG98 risk factor for significant jaundice.

A.q: Amira's baby is 10 hours old and the midwife notices yellow sclerae. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Use a transcutaneous bilirubinometer now
Recheck by eye in natural light at the next feed
Send a serum bilirubin urgently, within 2 hours
Send a serum bilirubin within the next 6 hours
A.why: Jaundice in the first 24 hours needs serum bilirubin measured urgently, within 2 hours, plus an urgent medical review within 6 hours (CG98 1.2.10, 1.2.12).

whyNot.0: Transcutaneous meters are not used in the first 24 hours of life (1.2.15).
whyNot.1: Visual inspection alone should not be relied on to estimate the level (1.2.6), and early jaundice needs urgent serum measurement.
whyNot.3: Within 6 hours is the time frame for babies over 24 hours old; under 24 hours it is 2 hours.

A.q: A term baby starts single phototherapy on the postnatal ward. Which care plan follows NICE guidance?
options: Supine, eye protection, short feeding breaks
Prone, so a larger area of skin is exposed
Extra water feeds between breastfeeds
White curtains around the cot to reflect light
A.why: CG98 1.4.12-1.4.15: place the baby supine, give eye protection, and encourage short breaks of up to 30 minutes for feeding, nappy changes and cuddles.

whyNot.1: NICE advises the supine position unless another condition prevents it.
whyNot.2: Breastfed babies should not be given additional fluids; expressed breast milk is the extra feed of choice if needed.
whyNot.3: White curtains are not used routinely because they may impair observation of the baby.

B.q: Noah is 40 hours old and was born at 36+4 weeks. His transcutaneous bilirubin reads 262 micromol/L. What should the midwife do next?
options: Start phototherapy on the TcB result
Repeat the TcB again in 18 hours
Arrange a serum bilirubin to check it
Advise the parents to watch his stools
B.why: When a transcutaneous reading is over 250 micromol/L, NICE advises measuring serum bilirubin to check the result (CG98 1.2.16).

whyNot.0: Treatment decisions at this level rest on a serum measurement, not the TcB reading.
whyNot.1: Repeating in 18 hours applies to a well baby below the threshold; a TcB over 250 needs serum confirmation now.
whyNot.3: Stool colour is checked in prolonged jaundice; this reading needs a serum level.

B.q: Which baby should have bilirubin measured by serum sample rather than with a transcutaneous meter?
options: A 30-hour-old baby born at 36 weeks
A 3-day-old baby born at 40 weeks
A 50-hour-old baby born at 38 weeks
A 2-day-old baby born at 33+6 weeks
B.why: Serum bilirubin is used for babies in the first 24 hours or with a gestational age under 35 weeks (CG98 1.2.15).

whyNot.0: Over 24 hours old and over 35 weeks, so a transcutaneous meter is appropriate.
whyNot.1: A term baby over 24 hours old can have a transcutaneous measurement.
whyNot.2: Over 24 hours and 38 weeks: transcutaneous measurement is the first choice.

B.q: A baby's serum bilirubin is falling under phototherapy. When should phototherapy be stopped?
options: When the level is just under the threshold
After a fixed course of 24 hours
When 50 micromol/L or more below threshold
When the skin no longer looks yellow
B.why: CG98 1.4.5: stop phototherapy once serum bilirubin has fallen at least 50 micromol/L below the phototherapy threshold, then check for rebound 12-18 hours later.

whyNot.0: Stopping just under the threshold risks rebound; NICE sets a 50 micromol/L margin.
whyNot.1: Duration depends on the bilirubin level, not a fixed time.
whyNot.3: Visual inspection is unreliable for estimating bilirubin, especially under phototherapy.

C.q: Ruby was born at 40 weeks and is exclusively breastfed. At 15 days she is still jaundiced and her mother mentions pale stools and dark urine staining the nappy. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure that breast milk jaundice is common
Arrange a conjugated bilirubin measurement
Advise more daylight exposure at home
Suggest replacing some feeds with formula
C.why: Jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby is prolonged; pale chalky stools and dark urine raise concern about liver disease, so conjugated bilirubin must be measured (CG98 1.7.1-1.7.2).

whyNot.0: Reassurance misses possible serious liver disease signalled by pale stools and dark urine.
whyNot.2: Sunlight is not a treatment for hyperbilirubinaemia (1.4.7).
whyNot.3: Changing feeds does not investigate the cause; breastfeeding can usually continue.

C.q: Kai was born at 35+2 weeks and is still visibly jaundiced on day 18. He is well and feeding. How should the midwife classify this?
options: Prolonged, as it has passed 14 days
Not yet prolonged; the limit is 21 days
Prolonged, as it has passed 10 days
Not yet prolonged; the limit is 28 days
C.why: For babies born before 37 weeks, jaundice is prolonged when it lasts more than 21 days (CG98 1.7.1). He still needs continued review.

whyNot.0: 14 days is the limit for babies born at 37 weeks or more.
whyNot.2: 10 days is not a CG98 threshold for prolonged jaundice.
whyNot.3: 28 days is the upper age limit of the guideline, not the prolonged jaundice threshold.

C.q: A 50-hour-old baby born at 39 weeks is under phototherapy. Which finding should make the team treat him as at increased risk of kernicterus?
options: Serum bilirubin of 290 micromol/L at 50 hours
Bilirubin rising 10 micromol/L per hour
Yellow colour visible on the gums
Exclusive breastfeeding every 3 hours
C.why: CG98 1.5.1: a rapidly rising bilirubin of more than 8.5 micromol/L per hour increases kernicterus risk, as do SBR over 340 micromol/L (37 weeks+) and signs of encephalopathy.

whyNot.0: The kernicterus marker for babies of 37 weeks or more is an SBR over 340 micromol/L.
whyNot.2: Gum colour helps detect jaundice but is not a kernicterus risk factor.
whyNot.3: Frequent breastfeeding is encouraged; it is not a kernicterus risk factor.

reteach.title: Two questions: how old, and how early?
reteach.question: Before you choose any test, ask the baby's age in hours and gestation. What do those two numbers tell you?

blocks.body: Jaundice that appears in the first 24 hours is never treated as routine: it may be haemolysis or infection. That baby needs a serum level within 2 hours and a doctor within 6. After 24 hours, measure within 6 hours. Gestation then decides the tool: 35 weeks or more and over a day old means a transcutaneous meter is fine; under 35 weeks or under a day old means a blood test.

blocks.text: Prolonged jaundice: 14 days for babies born at 37 weeks or more, 21 days for those born earlier. Pale chalky stools or dark urine at any point need prompt action.

explain.body: Everyone looks for jaundice: parents too. Examine the naked baby in bright, ideally natural light; check the sclerae and gums and blanch the skin. Colour change is harder to see in darker skin, and visual inspection alone is not relied on to estimate the level (CG98 1.2.4-1.2.6).

test.q: How should a midwife examine a baby for jaundice?
options: Naked baby, bright natural light, blanch the skin
Clothed baby, under the warm overhead cot lamp
Check the soles of the feet in dim light
Compare the skin colour against an icterometer card
test.why: CG98 1.2.5: check the naked baby in bright and preferably natural light, examining sclerae and gums and pressing lightly on the skin.

whyNot.1: A clothed baby under artificial warming light makes jaundice hard to see.
whyNot.2: Dim light hides the colour change; bright natural light is advised.
whyNot.3: NICE advises not to use an icterometer (1.2.17).

explain.body: Visible jaundice under 24 hours is a red flag for a pathological cause. Measure serum bilirubin within 2 hours, repeat every 6 hours until below threshold and stable or falling, and arrange urgent medical review within 6 hours (CG98 1.2.10-1.2.12).

test.q: A baby has visible jaundice at 20 hours. Alongside serum bilirubin within 2 hours, what does NICE require?
options: Routine NIPE review within 72 hours
Phototherapy started before any result
Repeat bilirubin every 12 hours
Urgent medical review within 6 hours
test.why: CG98 1.2.12: arrange an urgent medical review, as soon as possible and within 6 hours, to exclude pathological causes.

whyNot.0: The NIPE examination is routine; early jaundice needs an urgent medical review.
whyNot.1: Phototherapy is started when bilirubin exceeds the threshold, not before a result.
whyNot.2: Serum levels are repeated every 6 hours, not 12.

explain.body: A transcutaneous meter suits babies of 35 weeks or more who are over 24 hours old. Check any TcB over 250 micromol/L with serum, and use serum once at or above the treatment threshold. Use serum for babies under 24 hours or under 35 weeks (CG98 1.2.15-1.2.16).

test.q: Which baby is suitable for a transcutaneous bilirubin measurement?
options: A 12-hour-old baby born at 39 weeks
A 36-hour-old baby born at 37 weeks
A 30-hour-old baby born at 34 weeks
A baby already above the treatment line
test.why: At over 24 hours old and 35 weeks or more, a transcutaneous bilirubinometer is the recommended first measurement (CG98 1.2.16).

whyNot.0: Under 24 hours old needs serum bilirubin.
whyNot.2: Under 35 weeks gestation needs serum bilirubin.
whyNot.3: At or above the threshold, serum bilirubin is used for all measurements.

explain.body: During phototherapy repeat SBR 4-6 hours after starting, then every 6-12 hours when stable or falling. Stop at least 50 micromol/L below threshold and recheck 12-18 hours later for rebound. Prolonged jaundice (over 14 or 21 days) needs a conjugated bilirubin (CG98 1.4.4-1.4.6, 1.7.1).

test.q: A baby has just started phototherapy. When should the first repeat serum bilirubin be taken?
options: 12–18 hours after starting
Once daily at the same time
4–6 hours after starting
Every 2 hours until it falls
test.why: CG98 1.4.4: repeat serum bilirubin 4-6 hours after initiating phototherapy, then every 6-12 hours when stable or falling.

whyNot.0: 12-18 hours is the rebound check after phototherapy is stopped.
whyNot.1: Once daily is too infrequent for a baby starting treatment.
whyNot.3: Two-hourly sampling is not the recommended interval for single phototherapy.
